newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan telecom to spend 19bln rupees on network.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan telecom to spend 19bln rupees on network.

text.p: Pakistan's state-run telecom utility said on Tuesday it would spend 19 billion rupees ($468 million), including $250 million raised by securitisation of receivables, on a three-year network expansion plan.

Pakistan Telecommunications Company Ltd chairman Nasim Mirza told a news conference that PTCL had received $250 million last week from about a dozen foreign fund managers as a loan against its future income from bills other telephone carriers would pay it. The rest of the money will be raised from other sources, he said.

Most of the funds that gave the $250 million loan to PTCL were American and two were Japanese. "This is a unique deal," Mirza said. "In simple terms it is an advance against our future receivables. It is a loan against our future receivables."
The deal involves receivables from American Telephone and Telegraph Co, Sprint Corp, Mercury Communications Plc, MCI Communications Corp, British Telecommunications Plc and Deutsche Telekom AG.

Under the deal, the six carriers have certified to investors that the PTCL bills will be given to trustees, who would in turn deduct around nine percent interest against $250 million and pay investors.
Mirza said the $250 million would be given to the Pakistani government and the PTCL would get an equivalent amount in rupees to invest to expand its network.
"This is a deal which benefits not only PTCL but greatly benefits the government," Mirza said.
The PTCL plan includes expansion of the installed line capacity, laying of a submarine optical fibre cable from Karachi to the Far East and network modernisation.
PTCL has an installed capacity of 3.1 million lines, including 2.51 million working connections, and pending registered demand of 310,000 lines.
Mirza said last week's deal manifested international investors' confidence in the PTCL future incomes despite a proposed decline in international accounting rates.
Accounting rates decide how much telephone companies pay their counterparts in recipient countries for the cost of completing international calls.

The United States has led calls for a global deal to slash international accounting rates. It unilaterally slashed 50 percent of its own international settlement fees in December and started negotiations with various telecom operators.
Pakistan plans to privatise PTCL by selling a 26 percent stake and transfer its management to a strategic investor before the end of fiscal 1997/98 (July-June).
